📌 Watch-Only Wallets: Tracking Crypto Without Access to Funds

Main Points
⏺ A watch-only wallet lets users monitor balances and transactions without holding private keys
⏺ This setup is useful for large portfolios, cold storage, and address analysis
⏺ This post explains why monitoring assets doesn't require spending access

1️⃣ Core Idea — the app receives a public wallet address and displays its assets and transaction history.
2️⃣ Why It Helps — users can monitor long-term holdings without connecting the device that stores their private keys.
3️⃣ Use Cases — cold wallets, corporate treasuries, whale monitoring, and crypto portfolio accounting.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — the app cannot sign transactions without a key, but it may collect information about your addresses and financial activity.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — add only public addresses, verify supported networks, and never enter a seed phrase just to view balances.


Final Thoughts

You don't need to give an app control over your crypto just to monitor it. Separating viewing from signing reduces situations where private keys are exposed to unnecessary risk.

⭐️ Adam Back criticizes BIP-110 supporters after failed Bitcoin fork 

🌐 Blockstream CEO Adam Back has renewed his criticism of Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 110 (BIP-110), arguing that attempts to impose controversial network changes have repeatedly failed to gain market support. In a November 3 post on X, Back referenced earlier commentary from Bitcoin advocate Francis Pouliot while addressing supporters of the proposed Bitcoin fork.

📌 “Attempts to impose your views on bitcoin get market rejected,” Back wrote, pointing to previous disputes over Bitcoin’s rules. He described Pouliot’s commentary as a “masterclass on bitcoin reality” and said discussions about Bitcoin’s established rules were intended to help people understand immutability. Back’s latest comments followed renewed discussion about BIP-110, a proposal designed to restrict certain forms of non-financial data on Bitcoin.

➡️ He argued that the market would resist efforts to override consensus, even when supporters believed their proposed changes were beneficial.Back further claimed that BIP-110 “failed the first gate hard” because of what he described as serious technical problems. The criticism continued a position he adopted earlier this year, when he warned that the proposal could divide Bitcoin’s network.

Wall Street Turns on AI: Democrats’ Election Sweep Sends Shockwaves Through Tech Stocks 📉🏛


Wall Street is having second thoughts about the artificial intelligence boom. Following Democrats’ sweeping election victories, investors are rushing to unload shares of AI-related companies, raising fresh questions about the future of an industry that has become one of the biggest drivers of the U.S. stock market.

The sell-off reflects growing concerns that a stronger Democratic presence in government could change the political and regulatory landscape for artificial intelligence. At the center of the debate are data centers — the massive facilities powering the AI revolution. Their construction requires enormous amounts of electricity, water, land and capital, making them increasingly controversial in communities across the country.

Investors fear that tighter regulations, environmental restrictions and local opposition could slow down new projects, drive up costs and delay the expansion plans of major technology companies. For businesses that have committed billions of dollars to AI infrastructure, even modest delays could have serious financial consequences. 

The pressure is particularly significant for companies whose business models depend on rapid data-center expansion. 

Firms such as CoreWeave and Nebius have attracted investor attention because of their exposure to the booming demand for AI computing power. But their growth ambitions also make them vulnerable to rising borrowing costs, infrastructure bottlenecks and changes in government policy. The market is also confronting a deeper question: how much of the AI boom is justified by actual profits? 

Technology companies have poured staggering sums into chips, servers and computing facilities, betting that demand for artificial intelligence will continue to grow at an extraordinary pace. Yet investors are becoming less willing to accept ambitious promises without clear evidence of sustainable returns. Political uncertainty is adding another layer of risk. 

Democrats have increasingly raised concerns about the environmental impact of data centers, electricity prices and the concentration of power among major technology companies. A shift in political influence could translate into tougher oversight and a more challenging business environment for the sector.

The broader market fallout has been substantial, with technology valuations coming under renewed pressure. The reported losses in market capitalization underscore just how heavily investors had priced in an uninterrupted AI expansion.

Still, the sell-off does not necessarily signal the end of the artificial intelligence revolution. Rather, it may mark a turning point in how Wall Street evaluates the industry. Investors are beginning to distinguish between companies that can turn AI demand into reliable earnings and those whose valuations depend largely on expectations.

The message from the market is becoming increasingly clear: the AI boom may be far from over, but the days of treating every AI-related stock as an automatic winner could be coming to an end.

According to an October 27 Arkham Intelligence report, the tokens entered Sun-linked wallets over the previous 10 days, making him the largest individual PEPE holder outside cryptocurrency exchanges.

At the time, PEPE had a market capitalization of approximately $1.81 billion, with exchanges controlling several of the largest known holdings.

📊 Binance held $337.5 million worth of PEPE, representing 18.7% of the supply, followed by Robinhood with $150.9 million, or 8.37%.
